title: Unit 1a - From Java/Python to C++
summary: Title slide for CS103 Unit 1a covering the transition from Java and Python to C++ programming, authored by Mark Redekopp.
main_text: This is the introductory title slide for CS103 Unit 1a, which focuses on transitioning programming knowledge from Java or Python to C++. The unit covers fundamental C++ concepts including data types, constants, variables, input/output, expressions, and other basics that students coming from Java or Python need to learn when working with C++.
notes_text: This unit serves as a bridge for students who already know Java or Python and need to learn C++ syntax and concepts. The material assumes prior programming experience in at least one of these languages.

title: Review C++ Program Structure
summary: Shows the basic structure of a C++ program including #include directive, namespace declaration, and the main function with cout output.
main_text: A C++ program requires several key components. First, the #include <iostream> directive allows access to the cout object for output. The 'using namespace std;' statement avoids having to prefix standard library components with 'std::'. Every C++ program must have a main() function where execution begins. The main function returns an int type. Inside main, 'cout << "Hello world" << endl;' prints text to the screen, and 'return 0;' indicates successful program termination. The code shown is: // iostream allows access to 'cout' #include <iostream> using namespace std; // Execution always starts at the main() function int main() { cout << "Hello world" << endl; return 0; }
notes_text: This is a review slide for students who may have seen basic C++ before. The #include directive is a preprocessor command that inserts the contents of the iostream header file. The main() function is the entry point for all C++ programs.

images.description: Code example showing a complete minimal C++ program with iostream include, namespace declaration, and main function that prints Hello world

title: Module 1: Types (Constants and Variables)
summary: Section divider introducing Module 1 which covers how to represent data using types, constants, and variables in C/C++.
main_text: This is a section divider slide introducing Module 1 of the unit. Module 1 focuses on types, constants, and variables - the fundamental building blocks for representing data in C/C++ programs. The subtitle reads 'Starting to represent data', indicating this module will cover how programmers store and work with different kinds of information in their programs.
notes_text: Understanding types is foundational to C++ programming because unlike Python, C++ requires explicit type declarations. This module will cover integer types, floating point types, character types, string types, and boolean types.

title: Basic Output via cout
summary: Demonstrates basic console output using cout with string literals and integer values, showing a common error with missing insertion operators.
main_text: The cout object is used for console output in C++. This slide shows a program that uses multiple cout statements to print text and numbers. The code demonstrates: 'cout << "some ";' prints text without a newline, 'cout << "text" << endl;' prints text followed by a newline, and 'cout << 103 1889 << endl;' is marked as 'Bad...Fix me!' because it is missing the insertion operator (<<) between the two integer values 103 and 1889. The correct version would be 'cout << 103 << 1889 << endl;' or 'cout << 103 << " " << 1889 << endl;' to include a space between them. The program includes #include <iostream> and using namespace std; at the top.
notes_text: This slide introduces a common beginner mistake: forgetting to use the << operator between consecutive values in a cout statement. Without the operator, the compiler will produce an error. Students should also note that cout does not automatically add spaces between values.

images.description: Code example showing basic cout usage with string literals and a deliberate error where two integers are written without the << operator between them

title: Printing Different Values and Types
summary: Explains how cout requires the insertion operator as a separator between values, demonstrates printing variables and computed values, and introduces the overloaded << operator.
main_text: The cout object requires appropriate use of the insertion operator << as a separator between consecutive values or different types of values. Key points: (1) cout does not add spaces between consecutive values - you must do so explicitly. (2) It is generally good practice to give descriptive text when outputting variables or computed numbers. (3) You may divide output over multiple cout statements; unless a newline is printed (with endl or '\n'), the next output statement resumes where the last one left off. The code example shows: int x = 103; with several cout attempts: 'cout << x 1889 << endl;' causes a Compile Error, 'cout << x << 1889 << endl;' works but with no spaces, and 'cout << x << " " << 1889 << endl;' is the best approach. The program also uses string msg = "minutes"; and computes 60*24*365 to show 'There are 525600 minutes in a year.' The output shows: 1031889, 103 1889, and There are 525600 minutes in a year. Important: The << operator has multiple (overloaded) meanings. In C it is used to shift bits, but C++ also uses it for output as the 'stream insertion' operator.
notes_text: The concept of operator overloading is introduced here. The << operator serves as both a bitwise left shift operator (from C) and a stream insertion operator in C++. Understanding this dual meaning is important for avoiding confusion later when studying bitwise operations.

images.description: Code example demonstrating proper and improper use of the << operator with cout, showing compile errors, output without spaces, and correct output with spaces

title: C++ Data Types
summary: Comprehensive code example demonstrating all major C++ data types including int, unsigned int, double, float, char, bool, and string with their declarations and output.
main_text: This slide presents a complete C++ program demonstrating all major data types. The declarations include: int a1 = -42 (try assigning 4000000000 to see what happens), unsigned int a2 = 4000000000 (try assigning -1 to see what happens), double b1 = 3.14, float b2 = 1.5 (double is PREFERRED over float), char c = 'a', char d = 97, bool e = true, string f = "abc", and a long string g containing the USC fight song. The output statements demonstrate how each type is printed: cout prints char variables as their character representation, and casting char to int shows the ASCII value. The expression c = c+1 changes 'a' to 'b' (since 'a'+1 = 98 = 'b' in ASCII). Boolean constants true and false are printed as 1 and 0 by default. The program also shows that char d = 97 stores the ASCII character 'a' since 97 is the ASCII code for 'a'.
notes_text: This is a comprehensive demonstration slide. Students should experiment with boundary values (like assigning 4000000000 to an int or -1 to unsigned int) to understand overflow behavior. The relationship between char and int types through ASCII is a key concept in C/C++.

images.description: Full C++ program showing declarations and output of all major data types with comments explaining expected behavior

title: C/C++ Data Types Overview
summary: Categorizes C/C++ data types into integer, floating point, string/text, and boolean types, explaining that types determine storage size and interpretation.
main_text: C/C++ types indicate how many bits (bytes) of storage (memory) are required and how to interpret the number being stored. The types are categorized as follows: Integer types include int, unsigned int, and char (more explanation later). Floating point types handle very large numbers like 6.02E23 and very small numbers like 6.626E-34, representing rational/real numbers using float or double (prefer double over float as it has a greater range of expressivity). String/Text types include char, char arrays, and strings. Boolean type uses bool (true/false). The slide notes that the next topic will cover how to write constants (aka 'literals') and declare variables of these types.
notes_text: This categorization is fundamental to understanding C++ programming. Unlike Python, where types are inferred dynamically, C++ requires the programmer to explicitly declare the type of each variable. The type determines both the amount of memory allocated and how the stored bits are interpreted.

title: Review: Constants (aka Literals)
summary: Covers constant syntax for integers, doubles, characters, C-strings, and booleans, including escape sequences and the null terminator for C-strings.
main_text: Constants (literals) in C/C++ have specific syntax for each type. Integer constants: 496, 10005, -234. Double constants: 12.0, -16., 0.23, 6.02E23, 4e-2 (both very large and very small numbers using fractions/decimals). Characters (char type) are enclosed in single quotes ('): printing characters like 'a', '5', 'B', '!'. Each quoted value is converted to an appropriate ASCII number (e.g. 'a' => 97). Non-printing special characters use escape sequences preceded by a backslash: '\n' (newline/enter), '\t' (tab), '\\' (slash), '\'' (apostrophe). C-Strings (note: there is also a C++ string type) consist of 0 or more characters between double quotes ("), such as "hi1\n", "12345", "b", "\tAns. is %d". C-strings end with a '\0' (null character, value 0) added as the last byte to delimit the end of the string. Boolean (C++ only): false and true, with physical representation 0 = false and non-zero (1, -5, 300) = true. Important warning: C/C++ handling of single characters and strings is different from most other languages and is a major source of confusion in C++.
notes_text: The distinction between single quotes (for chars) and double quotes (for strings) is critical in C/C++. Unlike Python where they are interchangeable, in C++ 'a' is a char (1 byte, value 97) while "a" is a C-string (2 bytes: 'a' followed by null terminator '\0'). This distinction catches many beginners off guard.

images.description: Memory layout diagram showing how a C-string is stored in memory with addresses 7420-7426, each byte containing a character value and its ASCII code, ending with null terminator

title: You're Just My Type - Exercise
summary: Interactive exercise asking students to identify whether constants are correctly matched with their C++ types, with solutions provided at the end of the slide packet.
main_text: This exercise asks students to indicate which constants are matched with the correct type. The table presents the following pairs to evaluate: 4.0 matched with int, 5 matched with int, 'a' matched with string, "abc" matched with string, 5. matched with double, 5 matched with char, "5.0" matched with double, '5' matched with int. Students must determine Right or Wrong for each pairing. Solutions are provided at the end of the slide packet (slide 62). This exercise tests understanding of how C++ interprets different literal formats - for example, 4.0 contains a decimal point so it is a double not an int, and 'a' uses single quotes so it is a char not a string.
notes_text: This is a self-assessment exercise. Common mistakes include confusing single-quoted characters (chars) with strings, not recognizing that a decimal point makes a number a double, and not understanding that double-quoted text is a C-string rather than a numeric type.

images.description: Table with columns for Constant, Type, and Right/Wrong, listing 8 constant-type pairs for students to evaluate

title: Motivation for Data Types
summary: Explains why data types are necessary by showing raw memory contents and demonstrating that types tell the computer how many bytes to read and how to interpret them.
main_text: The slide poses the question: how many data values are stored in a sequence of memory bytes, and what are their values? A row of binary values is shown (0110 0001, 0011 1001, 0000 1010, 0000 0000, 0011 0111, 0001 0010, 1000 0000, etc.) to illustrate that without type information, raw memory is ambiguous. C/C++ types indicate how many bits (bytes) of storage (memory) are required and how to interpret the number being stored. Two examples illustrate this: a char 'a' takes 1 byte and stores the value 61 (hex), while a double -3.75 takes 8 bytes with a completely different bit interpretation. The slide explains that humans and debuggers often show memory contents in base-16 (hexadecimal or hex) rather than binary because it is less to write and easier to visually take in. Everything is truly binary in the computer, but there is an easy and fast way to convert between binary and hex, so hex is shown.
notes_text: This is a key conceptual slide. The same sequence of bits could represent completely different values depending on the type used to interpret them. A char reads 1 byte, an int reads 4 bytes, and a double reads 8 bytes from the same memory. This is why C/C++ requires explicit type declarations.

images.description: Diagram showing raw binary memory contents in a row of 16 bytes, with arrows showing how a char reads 1 byte and a double reads 8 bytes from the same memory, with hexadecimal representation below

title: Limited Range of Data
summary: Code example using std::numeric_limits to demonstrate the maximum and minimum values for int, unsigned int, char, and bool types, and what happens at overflow.
main_text: This slide shows a C++ program that explores the range limits of various data types using std::numeric_limits. For int: x = std::numeric_limits<int>::max() shows the maximum int value, then x + 1 demonstrates overflow. Similarly for min() and x - 1. For unsigned int: y = std::numeric_limits<unsigned int>::max() and y + 1, y = min() and y - 1 show unsigned overflow behavior. For char: z = std::numeric_limits<char>::max() and z + 1, z = min() and z - 1. For bool: b = true shows max, b + 1 shows what happens; b = false shows min, b - 1 shows underflow. This demonstrates that each type has a fixed range determined by the number of bits allocated, and exceeding that range causes overflow or underflow.
notes_text: Understanding overflow is critical for writing safe C++ code. When an int reaches its maximum value (approximately 2.1 billion) and you add 1, it wraps around to a large negative number. Similarly, subtracting 1 from an unsigned int value of 0 wraps to the maximum unsigned value (approximately 4.3 billion). This is undefined behavior for signed types and defined wraparound for unsigned types.

images.description: Complete C++ program demonstrating numeric_limits for int, unsigned int, char, and bool, showing max/min values and overflow/underflow behavior

title: Finite Range of Numbers
summary: Uses a hotel room number analogy to explain why computers have a finite range of representable numbers, introducing the concept of overflow.
main_text: Recall: EVERYTHING in a computer is a number. The slide uses a hotel room number analogy: a hotel with 3-digit room numbers can have rooms 000-999 (1000 rooms). With 4-digit numbers, 0000-9999. For n-digit room numbers, the range is 0 to 10^n - 1. Key Idea: A fixed number of digits (or bits, for a computer) limits the range of numbers we can represent. What is 999+1? Obviously 1000, but if we limit ourselves to 3-digit numbers, the answer is 000! This is called overflow and it is a common issue programmers must account for. The number of digits available determines the range of numbers that can be represented. Photos of hotel room numbers (610 for 3-digit and 1337 for 4-digit) illustrate the concept visually.
notes_text: The hotel room analogy makes overflow intuitive. Just as a 3-digit odometer rolls over from 999 to 000, computer integers wrap around when they exceed their maximum value. This is why choosing the right data type size matters in C++ - using a type that is too small can lead to silent overflow bugs.

images.description: Photos of hotel room numbers showing a 3-digit room (610) and a 4-digit room (1337) to illustrate how the number of digits determines the range of possible values

title: Bits, Bytes, Words
summary: Defines bits, bytes, and words as fundamental units of computer memory, explaining their sizes and the ranges of values they can represent.
main_text: Computers store data as bits (binary digits) in units of memory with a fixed number of bits. A single bit can only represent 1 and 0. To represent more than just 2 values we need to use a combination or sequence of many bits. Computer hardware (memory) defines common, easily accessible units of a fixed size: A byte is defined as a group of 8 bits. A word varies in size but is usually 32 bits (4 bytes). For n-bit numbers, the range of values we can represent is 0 to 2^n - 1. For 8 bits, the range is 0 to 255. For 32 bits, the range is 0 to 4,294,967,295. Computer memory (storage) is broken into bytes, with 1 or more bytes representing data values. The slide shows visual representations of a single bit (1), a byte (01000001 - corresponding to a C++ char), and a word (two groups of 8 bits - corresponding to a C++ int), along with a memory device diagram showing addresses 0-3 each storing a byte of data.
notes_text: Understanding the relationship between bits, bytes, and words is essential for understanding data types in C++. A char is 1 byte (8 bits), an int is typically 1 word (4 bytes = 32 bits). The number of bits directly determines the range of values a type can hold.

images.description: Diagram showing the hierarchy from a single bit (1) to a byte (8 bits, like a C++ char) to a word (32 bits, like a C++ int), with a memory device showing addresses 0-3 each containing a byte

title: C/C++ Integer Data Types
summary: Reference table showing all C/C++ integer types with their sizes in bytes and bits, and their signed and unsigned ranges.
main_text: Integer variable types can be unsigned (positive-only, including 0) or signed (positive or negative). The reference table shows: char/unsigned char: 1 byte, 8 bits, signed range -128 to +127, unsigned range 0 to 255. short/unsigned short: 2 bytes, 16 bits, signed range -32768 to +32767, unsigned range 0 to 65535. int/unsigned int: 4 bytes, 32 bits, signed range approximately -2 billion to +2 billion, unsigned range 0 to approximately 4 billion. long long/unsigned long long (aka size_t): 8 bytes, 64 bits, signed range -8*10^18 to +8*10^18, unsigned range 0 to 16*10^18. The three integer types used 99% of the time are char, int, and unsigned int (highlighted in the table).
notes_text: This is a key reference slide students should bookmark. The most commonly used integer types are int (for general integers), unsigned int (for positive-only values like array indices), and char (for characters and small numbers). The size_t type (unsigned long long) is used by the standard library for sizes and indices.

images.description: Reference table showing C type (signed), C type (unsigned), bytes, bits, signed range, and unsigned range for char, short, int, and long long

title: Summary: C/C++ Floating Point Types
summary: Reference table for float and double types with their sizes and ranges, recommending double over float and warning about rounding errors.
main_text: The float and double types allow decimal representation (e.g. 6.125) as well as very large integers (+6.023E23). Float: 4 bytes, 32 bits, range of approximately +/-7 significant digits * 10^(+/-38). Double: 8 bytes, 64 bits, range of approximately +/-16 significant digits * 10^(+/-308). Best practices: Prefer double over float because many compilers will upgrade floats to doubles anyhow. Do not use floating-point if you do not need to because it suffers from rounding error and has some additional time overhead to perform arithmetic operations compared to integer arithmetic.
notes_text: Rounding error in floating point is a fundamental concept in computer science. For example, 0.1 cannot be represented exactly in binary floating point, which can lead to subtle bugs in calculations. This is why you should never compare floating point numbers for exact equality.

images.description: Table comparing float and double types showing bytes, bits, and range for each

title: Variables
summary: Code example demonstrating variable declarations, initialization, type mismatches, uninitialized variables, and global vs local scope.
main_text: This slide shows a C++ program illustrating several variable concepts. A global variable 'int data = -1;' is declared outside any function. Inside function f1(): 'int x = 42;' asks 'Does this work?' - yes, variables can be declared and initialized in one step. 'int y = -1;' is valid, then 'y = "abc";' attempts to assign a string to an int, which would cause a type error. 'double z;' declares z without initialization, so 'cout << z' would print garbage (a random value). 'int a;' is uninitialized, then 'a += 1;' increments an uninitialized variable, which is undefined behavior. In main(): a 'Dummy call' prints numbers 41-48, then f1() is called, and finally 'cout << a << " " << data << endl;' tries to access 'a' which is not in scope (it was local to f1), but 'data' is accessible because it is global.
notes_text: This slide introduces several important concepts simultaneously: variable initialization, type safety, uninitialized variable dangers, and scope. The deliberate errors in the code are meant to illustrate common mistakes. Students should note that using an uninitialized variable is undefined behavior in C++.

images.description: C++ program with deliberate errors showing global variable declaration, function with variable initialization issues, uninitialized variables, and scope problems

title: C/C++ Variables
summary: Explains variables as reserved memory locations with a name and type, requiring declaration before use, with an analogy to renting an apartment.
main_text: A variable is a reserved memory location that stores a value that can be read (retrieved) or written (changed) as often as desired, and associates a descriptive name (e.g. x) the programmer will use with that memory location (address) and the value stored in that location. It is like renting an apartment or storage unit. You must 'declare' (allocate) your variables before using/assigning to them. A variable is not allocated (aka 'in scope') until the computer executes the line with the declaration. The declaration must give the type of the variable and a name/identifier. Code example shows: 'gr = 'A';' is BAD because it must be declared first. 'char gr = 'A';' is GOOD - declaring 'gr'. 'int x;' declares x but uninitialized variables will have a random garbage value until initialized. Then 'x = 1;' initializes x's value to 1, and 'gr = 'B';' changes gr's value to 'B'. Difference from C: C required variables be declared at the beginning of a function before any operations. C++ relaxes this and allows declarations anywhere in the code. Variables are actually allocated in RAM when the program is run.
notes_text: The memory diagram on this slide shows how variables map to specific memory addresses in RAM. char gr = 'B' occupies a single byte at one address, while int x occupies four bytes starting at another address. Understanding this physical representation helps explain why types matter - they determine how much memory is reserved.

images.description: Memory diagram showing how variables map to RAM addresses, with char gr = 'B' as a single-byte variable and int x as a four-byte variable, alongside an analogy photo of storage units
labels: A picture of computer memory (aka RAM)

title: Scope
summary: Explains variable scope as visibility and lifetime, distinguishing between global variables (accessible everywhere) and local variables (only within their function).
main_text: Scope of a variable refers to its visibility (who can access it) and lifetime (how long the memory is reserved). There are 2 scopes covered here: Global variables are declared outside of any function and are visible to all the code/functions in the program. Local variables are declared inside of a function and are only visible in that function; they die when the function ends. The code example shows: 'int x=1;' is a global variable. In function add_x(int input), y and z are NOT visible (in scope), but x is accessible since it is global. The function returns (input + x). In main(), 'int y, z=5;' declares local variables - y is garbage, z is 5. 'z = add_x(z);' calls the function, and 'y += z;' is marked BAD because y was never initialized (contains garbage). After main() ends, y and z die. The comment '// input dies here' shows that function parameters also have local scope.
notes_text: Understanding scope is essential for avoiding bugs. A common mistake is trying to access a local variable from another function, or using an uninitialized local variable. Global variables persist for the entire program lifetime, while local variables are created when their function is called and destroyed when it returns.

images.description: Code example with a global variable x, a function add_x that uses the global, and main() with local variables y and z, with comments showing scope boundaries

title: Summary: C/C++ Variable Types
summary: Comprehensive summary of all C/C++ variable types with example declarations showing the relationship between variable names, types, and constant values.
main_text: A type indicates how many bits/bytes of storage (memory) are required and how to interpret the number being stored. Integer types are signed (numbers can be positive or negative) by default, or unsigned (positive-only, including 0). A character type (more on this later). Floating point types handle very large 6.02E23 and very small numbers 6.626E-34 using float or double. String/Text types include a single char (1 character), character arrays (C-Strings), or string (C++ string type). Boolean type uses bool (true/false). The code example shows declarations with annotations identifying which parts are the variable and which are the constant: int a = -1; (Variable = int a, Constant = -1), unsigned int b = 2; (Variable, Constant), char c = 'A'; (where 'A' = 65 in ASCII), float d1 = 1.5; (Variable, Constant), double d2 = 3.14; (Variable, Constant), char e[6] = "Hello"; (C-string), string f = "Goodbye"; (C++ string), bool g = true;
notes_text: This summary slide ties together all the type concepts from the module. The visual annotations showing which part is the variable and which is the constant help students parse declaration syntax. Note that char arrays require specifying the size (including room for the null terminator), while C++ strings manage their own memory.

images.description: Code example with visual annotations using boxes to highlight which parts of declarations are variables and which are constants

title: Summary: Common Variable Types
summary: Quick reference table of the five most common C++ variable types with their usage, sizes, and ranges, plus a code example.
main_text: Variables are declared by listing their type and providing a name. They can be given an initial value using the '=' operator. The reference table shows: char - 1 byte, 8 bits, used for text characters and small integer values, range ASCII characters / -128 to +127. bool - 1 byte, 8 bits, used for true/false values. int/unsigned int - 4 bytes, 32 bits, used for integer values, signed range -2 billion to +2 billion, unsigned range 0 to +4 billion. double - 8 bytes, 64 bits, used for rational/real values, range +/-16 significant digits * 10^(+/-308). string - 1 or more bytes, used for arbitrary text. The code example declares: int w = -400; double x = 3.7; char y = 'a'; bool z = false; and prints them with cout.

title: Assignment Operator (=)
summary: Introduces the assignment operator showing how it updates a variable's memory location, with a visual diagram of processor reading from and writing to memory.
main_text: The assignment operator ('=') updates what is stored in a variable's memory (storage location). The example code shows: int x = 1; int y = 2; x = y + 3; After execution, x contains 5 (the result of 2 + 3) and y still contains 2. The visual diagram shows Computer Memory as containers (like buckets) that hold values, and the Computer Processor as a chip that performs calculations. For x = 1: the value 1 is written (orange arrow pointing left into memory) to the container labeled x. For y = 2: similarly, 2 is written to y. For x = y + 3: the processor first reads y's value 2 from memory (white arrow pointing right), adds 3 using the processor (shown with a plus sign), then writes the result 5 back to x's memory location. The old value 1 in x is crossed out and replaced with 5.
notes_text: The visual metaphor of memory containers and a processor chip helps students understand the physical process behind assignment. The key insight is that assignment is a two-step process: first evaluate the right-hand side expression, then store the result in the left-hand side variable.

images.description: Diagram showing computer memory as labeled containers (buckets) for x and y, and a processor chip, with arrows showing data flow during assignment operations

title: Common Mistake: Forgetting to Assign
summary: Warns that without the assignment operator, computed values are lost, contrasting 'x + 1;' (discarded result) with 'x = x + 1;' (stored result).
main_text: Without assignment, values are computed and then forgotten. The slide contrasts two cases: 'x + 1;' takes x's value and adds 1 but DOES NOT update x (just throws the result away). After this statement, x still holds its original value 0. 'x = x + 1;' uses assignment, so x actually updates. The processor reads x's current value (0), computes 0 + 1, and stores the result (1) back into x. The visual diagram shows two 'Before/After' scenarios with bucket containers. In the first (wrong) case, x starts at 0 and remains 0 after 'x + 1;' - marked with a red X. In the second (correct) case, x starts at 0 and becomes 1 after 'x = x + 1;' - marked with a green checkmark.
notes_text: This is one of the most common beginner mistakes, especially for students coming from mathematics where 'x + 1' implies the result is used. In C++, an expression without assignment is evaluated but the result is discarded. The compiler may even warn about this with 'statement has no effect'.

images.description: Side-by-side comparison showing x + 1 (result discarded, x stays 0, marked wrong) versus x = x + 1 (result stored, x becomes 1, marked correct) with bucket diagrams

title: Assignment Operator (=) Summary
summary: Summarizes assignment syntax as variable = expression, emphasizing right-to-left evaluation and that = does not mean equality comparison.
main_text: Syntax: variable = expression; where variable is the Left Hand Side (LHS) and expression is the Right Hand Side (RHS). The arrow points from RHS to LHS indicating the direction of data flow. Key to understanding assignment: work right to left. It should be read as: Store the resulting value of <expression> into memory location of <variable>. Example: z = x + y - (2*z); If a variable appears on both sides, we use the old/current value of the variable on the RHS. For example: int x = 1; x = x + 3; The current value of x (1) is used on the right side, then 1 + 3 = 4 is computed, and 4 becomes the new value of x. Important: = does NOT mean 'compare for equality'; that is the == operator. The slide shows arrows from x = x + 3 pointing to 'new-value of x (4)' on the left and 'current-value of x (1)' on the right. The callout emphasizes: Evaluate everything on the right-hand side (RHS) before considering the left-hand side (LHS).
notes_text: The distinction between = (assignment) and == (equality comparison) is a fundamental source of bugs for beginners. Writing 'if (x = 5)' instead of 'if (x == 5)' will assign 5 to x and always evaluate as true, which is almost never the intended behavior.

images.description: Diagram showing the assignment x = x + 3 with arrows indicating that the current value of x (1) on the RHS is used to compute the new value of x (4) on the LHS

title: Important: Assignment Means Copy
summary: Explains that assignment copies values between variables, leaving the source unchanged, and demonstrates why order matters through a failed swap attempt.
main_text: Assigning a variable makes a copy. It leaves the source variable unchanged and is performed immediately, taking effect before the next statement. Order/sequence MATTERS - one assignment statement affects subsequent expressions. The first example: int x = 5, y = 3; x = y; copies y into x, so x becomes 3 while y still has 3. Challenge: Swap the value of 2 variables. The naive approach with int a = 7, b = 9: a = b; b = a; does NOT work. After 'a = b;', both a and b contain 9. Then 'b = a;' copies 9 into b, so both still contain 9 - the original value of a (7) is lost. The visual diagram shows boxes for a and b, with a going from 7 to 9 after the first assignment, and b remaining 9 after the second, demonstrating the failed swap.
notes_text: This is a classic programming problem that illustrates why understanding assignment as a copy operation is critical. The naive swap fails because the first assignment overwrites a's original value before it can be saved. The solution (shown on the next slide) requires a temporary variable.

images.description: Visual diagram showing boxes for variables x, y, a, and b, demonstrating how assignment copies values and how a naive swap attempt fails because the original value is overwritten

title: More Assignments - Swap with Temporary Variable
summary: Shows the correct way to swap two variables using a third temporary variable, with step-by-step visual tracking of values.
main_text: Assigning a variable makes a copy, leaving the source variable unchanged. To swap the value of 2 variables, the easiest method is to use a 3rd temporary variable to save one value and then replace that variable. The code example: int a = 7, b = 9, temp; Step 1: temp = a; (temp gets 7, a still has 7, b still has 9). Step 2: a = b; (a gets 9, b still has 9, temp still has 7). Step 3: b = temp; (b gets 7, now a=9 and b=7 - swap complete). The program then prints: cout << a << " " << b << endl; which outputs '9 7'. The visual diagram shows three boxes labeled a, b, and temp, with numbered circles (1, 2, 3) indicating the order of operations, and arrows showing the flow of values through each step.
notes_text: The three-variable swap is a fundamental algorithm pattern. While C++ provides std::swap() in the standard library, understanding the manual approach teaches important concepts about how assignment works. A challenge extension (4swap exercise) is mentioned for further practice.

images.description: Step-by-step diagram with boxes for a, b, and temp showing values at each stage of the swap, with numbered circles indicating operation order and code alongside

title: Shortcut Assignment Statements
summary: Introduces compound assignment operators (+=, -=, *=, /=, %=) as shorthand for updating a variable by applying an operation to its current value.
main_text: A common task is to update a variable by adding, subtracting, multiplying, etc. some value to it. For example: x = x + 4; and y = y * 2.5; C/C++ provide a shortcut for writing these statements: x += 4; and y *= 2.5; The substitution rule is: var op= expr; becomes var = var op expr; Shorthand operators exist for most operators: +=, -=, *=, /=, %=, &=, and more. The code example demonstrates: int x = 1; double y = 3.75; x += 5; (x updates to 6), y -= 2.25; (y updates to 1.5), x /= 3; (x updates to 2), y *= 2.0; (y updates to 3.0). The program outputs these values to verify the results.
notes_text: Compound assignment operators are not just syntactic sugar - they can be more efficient in some cases because the variable is only looked up once. They are also less error-prone because you only write the variable name once, reducing the chance of typos in complex expressions.

images.description: Code example showing compound assignment operators with int and double variables, with comments showing the resulting values after each operation

title: Module 2: C++ I/O (Input/Output)
summary: Section divider introducing Module 2 which covers inputting and outputting data in C++ programs.
main_text: This is a section divider slide introducing Module 2 of the unit. Module 2 focuses on C++ I/O (Input/Output) - the mechanisms for getting data into and out of a C++ program. The subtitle reads 'Inputting and outputting data', indicating this module will cover cin for keyboard input and cout for screen output, as well as related topics like I/O streams, manipulators, and handling whitespace.
notes_text: I/O is fundamental to interactive programming. This module will build on the basic cout usage from Module 1 and introduce cin for reading user input. Understanding how C++ handles I/O streams is important for both console applications and file processing.

title: I/O Streams
summary: Explains how C++ uses cin and cout objects to access input and output streams (stdin/stdout), with diagrams showing the flow of data between keyboard, OS, and screen.
main_text: C++ and the OS use the notion of streams to temporarily store (aka buffer) data to be input or output, and then uses the cin and cout objects (from the <iostream> library) to access those streams. The cin object extracts data from the input stream [stdin] (skipping over preceding whitespace then stopping at following whitespace). The cout object inserts data into the output stream [stdout] for display by the OS. The diagram shows the data flow: for output, cout inserts characters into the output stream memory (stdout), such as 'I t w a s t h e \n b e', and the OS then displays the text on screen. Example code: std::cout << "It was the" << std::endl; std::cout << "best of times."; For input, the keyboard sends characters to the OS which stores them in the input stream memory (stdin), such as '7 5 y ...', and cin reads from this buffer. Example code: int x; std::cin >> x; reads the value from the input stream.
notes_text: The stream model is a key abstraction in C++ I/O. Streams act as buffers between the program and the hardware (keyboard/screen). This buffering allows the OS to handle the timing of actual hardware I/O independently from the program's execution. The std:: prefix can be avoided by using 'using namespace std;'.

images.description: Diagram showing data flow from keyboard through OS to input stream (cin) and from output stream (cout) through OS to screen display, with example code snippets

title: I/O Manipulators
summary: Introduces output formatting manipulators including setw, setprecision, fixed, and boolalpha from the iomanip library.
main_text: Manipulators control HOW cout handles certain output options and how cin interprets the input data (but print nothing themselves). You must #include <iomanip> to use them. Common manipulators: setw(n) separates consecutive outputs by n spaces. setprecision(n) uses n digits to display doubles (both the integral and decimal parts). fixed uses the precision for only the digits after the decimal point. boolalpha shows Booleans as 'true' and 'false' rather than 1 and 0. Manipulators are separated by << or >> and used inline with actual data. Other than setw, manipulators continue to apply to later output until changed. The code example demonstrates: double pi = 3.14159; cout << pi << endl; prints 3.14159. cout << setprecision(2) << pi << endl; prints 3.1. cout << setprecision(2) << fixed << pi << endl; prints 3.14. Reference: http://en.cppreference.com/w/cpp/io/manip
notes_text: The persistence behavior of manipulators is important to understand. setw only affects the next output operation, while setprecision and fixed remain in effect until explicitly changed. This can lead to unexpected formatting if students forget that a manipulator is still active from earlier in the code.

images.description: Code example showing the effect of different manipulators on printing the value of pi, with comments showing the output for each configuration

title: endl and Flushing - Code Example
summary: Shows a code example with a function that may crash, demonstrating the importance of flushing output for debugging purposes.
main_text: This slide shows a code example that sets up the discussion about endl and flushing. The program includes <iostream>, <iomanip>, and <cmath>, and declares a function prototype: void task_that_may_crash(bool x); In main(), the function is called twice: first with false (does not crash), printing 'A\n', then with true (does crash), printing 'B\n'. This example is used to illustrate why flushing matters - if the output is not flushed before a crash, the last debug message may not appear on screen, making it difficult to determine where the program crashed.
notes_text: This slide introduces the concept with a minimal example before the full explanation on the next slides. The key question is: if the program crashes during the second call to task_that_may_crash(true), will 'A' be visible on screen? The answer depends on whether the output was flushed.

images.description: C++ code showing a program that calls a potentially crashing function twice with different boolean arguments, printing A and B between calls

title: Newlines, endl, and Flushing
summary: Explains the difference between '\n' and endl, how cout buffers output, and why flushing is important for debugging crashes.
main_text:
To move the cursor to the next line we need to print a new line character '
' (char). cout only gives the characters to the OS which then copies them to the screen. The OS may choose to delay and not print immediately, causing strange issues (see bottom). endl = '
' + a flush of the output stream which forces the OS to print immediately. The visual diagram shows two scenarios with cartoon characters representing cout and OS: With 'cout << "Hi
";' - cout asks the OS 'could you print this for me?' and the OS responds 'Pshh! I'm busy. Maybe I'll do it now, maybe later.' - the screen remains blank. With 'cout << "Hi" << endl;' - cout says 'Could you print this for me. Oh and btw, I'm flushing!' and the OS responds 'Your wish is my command!' - the screen shows 'Hi'.
notes_text: The flushing concept is crucial for debugging. When a program crashes, any unflushed output in the buffer is lost. Using endl instead of '\n' ensures that output appears on screen before the next statement executes, which helps identify where a crash occurred.

images.description: Two-panel cartoon diagram showing cout and OS interaction: with \n the OS may delay printing, but with endl the OS prints immediately due to flushing

title: Newlines, endl, and Flushing - Debugging Example
summary: Demonstrates with a concrete crash scenario why using endl instead of \n is essential for debugging, showing how unflushed output is lost on crash.
main_text:
This slide continues the explanation of flushing with a practical debugging example. The same concepts are repeated at top: '
' is just a newline character, cout buffers output, the OS may delay printing, and endl = '
' + flush. Two side-by-side code examples show the difference. Without endl (using 
): task_that_might_crash() does not crash, cout << "Got Here 1
"; then task_that_might_crash() DOES crash. Output shows only <Segmentation fault> with no debug messages - 'Got Here 1' was in the buffer but never flushed before the crash. With endl: same code but using endl, cout << "Got Here 1" << endl;. Output shows 'Got Here 1' followed by <Segmentation fault>. Because endl flushed the buffer, the debug message appeared before the crash. The callout emphasizes: Use descriptive messages and endls when debugging.
notes_text: This is one of the most practical debugging tips in the course. When tracking down crashes, always use endl (not just \n) so that debug print statements actually appear on screen before the crash occurs. Otherwise, you may be misled about where the crash happened because the output was still in the buffer.

images.description: Side-by-side comparison of debugging output: left shows program using \n where debug message is lost on crash, right shows program using endl where debug message appears before crash

title: Input with cin
summary: Shows a complete example of reading user input with cin, including string and int variables, with conditional output based on the input.
main_text: This slide presents a complete interactive program using cin for input. The program includes <iostream> and <iomanip>. It declares: string name; int age; Then prompts: cout << "Enter your first name and age: " << endl; The input is read with: cin >> name >> age; The program then uses a conditional: if(age >= 18) it prints the name followed by ', you are allowed to vote in the next election.' Otherwise it prints the name followed by ', wait ' and the number of years remaining (18-age) and ' more years to vote.' This demonstrates how cin reads multiple values of different types in sequence, and how the input values can be used in expressions and conditionals.
notes_text: This example shows a realistic use case for cin. Note that cin >> name will only read a single word (up to the first whitespace). If the user types 'John Doe 25', name would get 'John', and the program would try to read 'Doe' as the age, causing an error. Reading full lines requires getline().

images.description: Complete C++ program showing cin reading a name and age, then using an if-else conditional to print different messages based on whether the user is old enough to vote

title: Coming From Java
summary: Brief comparison noting that cin works similarly to Java's Scanner class with nextInt(), nextLine(), and nextFloat() methods.
main_text: If you come from Java, cin works most similarly to the Scanner class with its nextInt(), nextLine(), nextFloat() methods. Just as Scanner reads from standard input and parses values based on the expected type, cin uses the >> operator to extract typed values from the input stream. The extraction operator automatically handles type conversion based on the variable type on the right side of >>.
notes_text: This is a helpful bridge for Java students. In Java, Scanner.nextInt() reads an integer, Scanner.nextDouble() reads a double, etc. In C++, cin >> x automatically determines whether to read an int, double, or string based on the declared type of x. The behavior regarding whitespace skipping is also similar.

title: Input with cin - Multiple Types
summary: Demonstrates reading multiple values of different types (char, int, double, string) in a single cin chain using the >> operator.
main_text: This program demonstrates reading multiple values of different types using cin. Variable declarations: char w; int x; double y; string z; The prompt asks: 'Enter a char, int, double, and string:' and the input is read with a single chained statement: cin >> w >> x >> y >> z; This reads four values in sequence from the input stream, automatically converting each to the appropriate type based on the variable declaration. The output displays all four values separated by spaces: cout << w << " " << x << " " << y << " " << z << endl; This demonstrates that the >> operator can be chained just like the << operator with cout, and that cin handles type conversion automatically.
notes_text: Chaining multiple >> operators is convenient but requires the user to enter values in the correct order and type. Each >> skips leading whitespace and reads until the next whitespace character. If the user enters a value that cannot be converted to the expected type, cin enters an error state.

images.description: C++ program showing cin reading four different types (char, int, double, string) in a single chained statement and printing them back

title: Keyboard Input
summary: Explains how the cin object receives keyboard input through the OS input stream, with a detailed flow diagram and note about the overloaded >> operator.
main_text: In C++, the 'cin' object is responsible for receiving input from the keyboard. Keyboard input is captured and stored by the OS (in an 'input stream') until cin is called upon to 'extract' info into a variable in your program. 'cin' converts text input to the desired format (e.g. integer, double, etc.). The code example: int dozens; cout << "Enter number of dozen: " << endl; cin >> dozens; cout << 12 * dozens << " eggs" << endl; The diagram shows the data flow: user types on keyboard, OS captures the input (e.g. '1 5 \n'), stores it in the input stream, cin extracts the value '15' and stores it in the variable 'dozens'. After extraction, '\n' remains in the input stream. Important: The >> operator also has multiple (overloaded) meanings. In C (and still in C++) it is used to shift bits in a variable to the right, but C++ also uses it for input. In the input context, it is NOT known as the shift operator but the 'stream extraction' operator.
notes_text: The diagram is key to understanding cin's behavior. Note that after cin extracts a value, the remaining characters (including the trailing newline) stay in the input stream buffer. This leftover data can affect subsequent cin operations, which is a common source of bugs.

images.description: Flow diagram showing keyboard input going through OS to input stream buffer, then cin extracting the numeric value into a variable, with remaining characters left in the stream

title: Dealing With Whitespace
summary: Explains how cin handles whitespace: skipping leading whitespace and stopping at the first trailing whitespace, with a visual stream diagram.
main_text:
Whitespace is defined as characters that represent horizontal or vertical blank space. Examples: newline ('
'), TAB ('	'), spacebar (' '). cin sequentially discards leading whitespace characters until it hits a non-whitespace character. cin then checks if the characters can be converted to the appropriate variable type and keeps scanning for more. cin will STOP at the first trailing whitespace (or on a character unable to be converted to the desired type) and await the next cin command. The code example shows: int dozens; cout << "Enter number of dozen: " << endl; cin >> dozens; When the user types '	 1 5 
' (tab, space, 1, 5, newline), cin skips the leading tab and space, reads '15' into dozens (value 15), and stops at the trailing '
' which remains in the input stream. Main take-aways: cin SKIPS leading whitespace. cin STOPS on the first trailing whitespace. Important: Space is not equal to Whitespace (Whitespace = ' ', '	', '
', etc.).
notes_text: Understanding cin's whitespace behavior is essential for debugging input issues. The fact that cin leaves trailing whitespace in the stream is the root cause of many input bugs, especially when mixing cin >> with getline(). The distinction between 'space' and 'whitespace' is important - whitespace includes tabs, newlines, and other non-printable characters.

images.description: Diagram showing the input stream with tab, space, 1, 5, and newline characters, with cin extracting 15 into the dozens variable and leaving \n in the stream

title: Multiple Inputs and Unexpected Inputs
summary: Shows how to chain multiple cin extractions and notes that programs assume users enter correctly formatted input.
main_text: Use the '>>' operator to separate any number of variables you want to read. For now, let us make the unreasonable assumption that the user always types in the right 'format' of information. We will learn more about how cin handles errors later. The code example: int score; double multiplier; cin >> score >> multiplier; When the user types '15 2.4', cin reads 15 into score (int) and 2.4 into multiplier (double). The diagram shows the input stream containing '\t 1 5 2 . 4 \n', with cin extracting 15 and 2.4 into their respective variables, leaving '\n' in the stream. The output: cout << "Your new score is " << score * multiplier << endl; prints 'Your new score is 36'. The program produces the expected result when user input matches the expected format.
notes_text: The assumption that users always provide correctly formatted input is unrealistic but simplifies initial learning. Error handling for cin will be covered later in the course. When reading multiple values, cin uses whitespace as a delimiter between values.

images.description: Diagram showing input stream with user-typed values being extracted by cin into int and double variables, with the remaining newline left in the stream

title: Timing of Execution
summary: Explains that cin either waits for keyboard input when the stream is empty or immediately extracts from the stream if data is already available.
main_text:
When execution reaches a 'cin' statement, it will either: Wait for input if nothing is available in the input stream (the OS will capture what is typed until the next Enter key is hit, then the user can type as little or much as desired until Enter), or Immediately extract from the input stream if some text is already available and convert it to the desired type of data. The code example demonstrates: cin >> dozens; reads from an empty stream, so the program waits for user input. The user types '15 3.7
'. cin reads 15 into dozens and leaves '3.7
' in the stream. Later, cin >> gpa; finds '3.7
' already in the stream, so it immediately extracts 3.7 without waiting for new input. This shows that a single line of user input can satisfy multiple cin calls if enough data is available in the stream.
notes_text: This is a crucial concept for understanding cin behavior. Students often expect each cin call to prompt the user for new input, but cin only waits if the input stream is empty. If previous input left data in the stream, cin reads from there first. This can cause confusing behavior where input seems to be 'skipped'.

images.description: Two-state diagram showing cin first waiting for input (empty stream), then immediately extracting from a stream that already contains data from a previous user entry
labels: No input available. Wait for user to type and hit Enter

title: Unexpected Inputs
summary: Demonstrates what happens when cin receives input that cannot be converted to the expected type, resulting in variables retaining garbage values.
main_text: The '>>' operator can be used to input any number of variables you want to read. If unexpected non-whitespace characters are encountered, cin simply stops and leaves the variable values unchanged. It does not discard the unexpected characters, so they will likely cause another error on the next read, too. More on error handling and input validation in CS103. The code example shows: double b, h; cin >> b >> h; When user types 'xy 1.25 2', the input stream contains 'x y 1 . 2 ...' and cin tries to read a double but encounters 'x', which cannot be converted to a number. Both b and h get garbage values (shown as '??'). The output shows 'Area of rect: 5.428E35' and 'Area of triangle: 2.714E35' - clearly wrong results from using uninitialized/garbage values in calculations.
notes_text: This slide demonstrates a real-world failure mode. When cin fails to parse input, it enters an error state and all subsequent cin operations fail silently. The unconsumed characters remain in the stream, propagating the error. Students need to be aware of this behavior even though formal error handling comes later.

images.description: Diagram showing cin trying to read doubles but encountering letter characters, resulting in garbage values being used in calculations that produce nonsensical output

title: cin Question - Type Mismatch Behavior
summary: Asks what happens when a double is entered for an integer variable and when numeric digits are entered for a string variable, showing cin's parsing behavior.
main_text: What do you think would happen if the user typed a double when an integer was expected? cin will stop on the decimal point ('.'). What happens if you type numeric digits when a string is expected? Numeric digits can be part of a string, so cin simply reads all characters through the first whitespace. The code example: int x; cin >> x; and the user types '1.5 42'. cin reads 1 into x (stops at '.'), leaving '.5 42\n' in the stream. Then double y, z; cin >> y >> z; reads .5 into y and 42 into z from the remaining stream data. Then string s; cin >> s; and user types '103.25'. Since a string can contain any characters, cin reads '103.25' as a complete string (stops at whitespace). Output: x = 1 (not shown but implied), y,z = 0.5 42 (remaining from first input), s = 103.25.
notes_text: This is the same content as slide 63 but presented as a question first for active learning. The key insight is that cin >> int stops at any non-digit character (like '.'), and those unconsumed characters remain in the stream for subsequent reads. This cascading behavior is a major source of confusion for beginners.

images.description: Step-by-step diagram showing how cin parses '1.5 42' when reading into an int then doubles, with the input stream state shown at each stage

title: std:: and the using namespace statement
summary: Explains that C++ library components live in the std namespace, and the 'using namespace std;' statement avoids having to write std:: before every library call.
main_text: Most C++ library components 'live' in the std namespace. Think of a namespace like folders on your laptop or a classification hierarchy. So cout and endl are technically std::cout and std::endl. To avoid all that typing, we can tell the C++ compiler to look for components in the std namespace when it cannot find any definition earlier in our code by writing 'using namespace std;'. Two code examples demonstrate the difference: With 'using namespace std;', you can write 'cout << "It was the" << endl;'. Without it, you must write 'std::cout << "It was the" << std::endl;'. A visual diagram shows a folder hierarchy with '/' at the top, containing 'std' folder, which contains 'cout', 'endl', and 'cin'. Demo suggestion: Try to compile a program WITHOUT the using statement to see the error message.
notes_text: The 'using namespace std;' directive is convenient for beginners but considered bad practice in larger projects because it can cause name collisions. In professional C++ code, you will often see explicit std:: prefixes or selective 'using std::cout;' declarations instead of importing the entire namespace.

images.description: Folder hierarchy diagram showing the root '/' containing the 'std' folder, which contains cout, endl, and cin as items within the namespace

title: Error without 'using' statement
summary: Shows the actual compiler error message when cout is used without 'using namespace std;' or the std:: prefix.
main_text: This slide demonstrates the actual compiler error that occurs when the 'using namespace std;' statement is commented out. The code file lec02-cout.cpp contains: #include <iostream>, //using namespace std; (commented out), int main() { cout << "Hello world" << endl; return 0; }. When compiled with 'make lec02-cout' (which runs g++ lec02-cout.cpp -o lec02-cout), the compiler produces the error: 'lec02-cout.cpp: In function 'int main()': lec02-cout.cpp:6:5: error: 'cout' was not declared in this scope; did you mean 'std::cout'?'. The error message helpfully suggests using 'std::cout' as the fix. The code editor screenshot shows the error highlighted on line 6 where cout is used.
notes_text: This is a very common error for beginners. The compiler error message is quite helpful in this case, suggesting std::cout as the correct identifier. Students should learn to read and interpret compiler error messages, as they often contain the solution to the problem.

images.description: Screenshot of a code editor showing a C++ file with 'using namespace std' commented out, and the terminal below showing the resulting compiler error about cout not being declared in scope
labels: error: 'cout' was not declared in this scope

title: Module 3: Expressions
summary: Section divider introducing Module 3 which covers performing computation with expressions in C++.
main_text: This is a section divider slide introducing Module 3 of the unit. Module 3 focuses on Expressions - the mechanisms for performing computation in C++ programs. The subtitle reads 'Performing computation', indicating this module will cover arithmetic operators, operator precedence, division behavior, casting, and other expression-related topics.
notes_text: Expressions are combinations of variables, constants, and operators that evaluate to a value. Understanding how C++ evaluates expressions - especially with integer division, operator precedence, and type promotion - is essential for writing correct calculations.

title: Expressions and Operators
summary: Code example demonstrating modulo, integer division, floating-point division, update assignment operators, and pre/post increment/decrement.
main_text: This slide shows a comprehensive C++ program demonstrating various expression operators. The code initializes int x = 7, y = 5, z = 12; and demonstrates: Modulo operations: 7 % 5 = 2 and 7 % 12 = 7. Integer division: 7 / 5 = 1 (truncated). Floating-point division: 7 / 5.0 = 1.4 and x / 5.0 produces a double result. Update assignment operators: x += 1 increments x, x /= 2 divides x by 2. Pre/post increment and decrement: z++ (post-increment: use then increment), z-- (post-decrement: use then decrement), ++z (pre-increment: increment then use), --z (pre-decrement: decrement then use). Each operation is printed with cout to show the result.
notes_text: This code is meant to be compiled and run by students to observe the behavior. The distinction between integer and floating-point division is crucial, as is the difference between pre and post increment/decrement when used in larger expressions.

images.description: Complete C++ program demonstrating modulo, integer/floating-point division, compound assignment, and pre/post increment/decrement operations with cout output

title: Arithmetic Operators
summary: Reference table of the five arithmetic operators (+, -, *, /, %) with examples, noting the difference between integer and double division.
main_text: Addition, subtraction, and multiplication work as expected for both integer and floating point types. Division works 'differently' for integer vs. doubles/floats. Modulus is only defined for integers. The reference table shows: + (Addition, example: 2 + 5), - (Subtraction, example: 41 - 32), * (Multiplication, example: 4.23 * 3.1e-2), / (Division with Integer vs. Double division, examples: 10 / 3 = 3 for integers, 10.0 / 3 = 3.3333 for doubles), % (Modulus/remainder for integers only, example: 17 % 5 = 2, result will be 2). Practice problems at the bottom: 17 % 10 = __ and 4 % 7 = __ (answers: 7 and 4).
notes_text: The modulus operator % returns the remainder after integer division. It only works with integer operands. Common uses include checking if a number is even (n % 2 == 0), extracting digits, and implementing circular/wrapping behavior. Division is the trickiest operator because its behavior changes based on operand types.

images.description: Table listing the five arithmetic operators with their symbols, names, and examples showing the distinction between integer and floating-point division

title: Division
summary: Explains the critical difference between integer division (truncates remainder) and floating-point division (preserves decimals), including implicit casting in mixed expressions.
main_text: Computers perform division differently based on the type of values used as inputs. Integer Division: When dividing two integral values, the result will also be an integer (any remainder/fraction will be dropped). Examples: 10 / 4 = 2, 52 / 10 = 5, 6 / 7 = 0. Floating-point (Double) and Mixed Division: When at least one operand is a double/float, the result preserves the decimal. Examples: 10.0 / 4.0 = 2.5, 52.0 / 10 = 5.2, 6 / 7.0 = 0.8571. Important note: If one input is a double, the other will be promoted temporarily (aka implicitly casted) to the more expressive type to compute the result as a double. This means 6 / 7.0 promotes the integer 6 to 6.0 before dividing.
notes_text: Integer division truncation is one of the most common sources of bugs in C++ programs. The expression 1/3 evaluates to 0, not 0.333. This catches many beginners off guard, especially in formulas like computing averages. The implicit casting rule (promotion to the more expressive type) is a safety mechanism but can still lead to surprises.

title: Precedence
summary: Covers operator precedence (order of operations) with a comprehensive reference table of all C++ operators ranked by priority level and associativity.
main_text: Precedence determines the order of operations/evaluation of an expression. Higher levels (e.g. level 16 in table) are done first. Operations with the same level or precedence usually are evaluated left to right (with some exceptions having right-to-left associativity). Practice: Evaluate 2*-4-3+5/2; should be computed as (2*(-4)) - 3 + (5/2) = -8 - 3 + 2 = -9. Tips: Use parentheses to add clarity. Add a space between literals, e.g. (2 * -4) - 3 + (5 / 2). The reference table shows all C++ operators from level 16 (highest: scope resolution ::) to level 1 (lowest: comma operator). Key levels include: Level 15: function calls, array subscript, postfix ++/--. Level 14: prefix ++/--, unary +/-, logical/bitwise NOT, casts, sizeof. Level 13: multiplication, division, modulo. Level 12: addition, subtraction. Level 10: relational operators (<, <=, >, >=). Level 9: equality (==, !=). Level 5: logical AND (&&). Level 4: logical OR (||). Level 2: assignment operators (=, +=, -=, etc.).
notes_text: Students do not need to memorize the entire precedence table, but should know the most common levels: parentheses first, then unary operators, then */% before +-, then comparisons, then logical operators, then assignment. When in doubt, use parentheses to make the intended evaluation order explicit.

images.description: Comprehensive C++ operator precedence table showing all operators organized by priority level (16 highest to 1 lowest) with their descriptions and associativity direction

title: Exercise Review - Expression Evaluation
summary: Practice exercise asking students to evaluate three arithmetic expressions applying integer division and operator precedence rules.
main_text: This exercise asks students to evaluate the following expressions: 25 / 3 (integer division, answer is 8 since both operands are integers). 17 + 5 % 2 - 3 (modulus has higher precedence than + and -, so 5 % 2 = 1, then 17 + 1 - 3 = 15). 28 - 5 / 2.0 (division has higher precedence than subtraction, and since 2.0 is a double, 5/2.0 = 2.5, then 28 - 2.5 = 25.5). These exercises are from D.S. Malik, C++ Programming, 5th Ed., Ch. 2, Q6.
notes_text: These exercises test three key concepts: integer division truncation (25/3 = 8 not 8.33), operator precedence (% before +/-), and mixed-type division (int/double = double). Students should work through these carefully before checking answers on the solutions slide.

title: Casting (C and C++ Style)
summary: Code example demonstrating type casting between numeric types and strings, showing both static_cast and string conversion functions.
main_text: This slide shows a C++ program demonstrating various casting operations. With numeric types: int x = 3, y = 2; double z = x/y; results in z = 1 (integer division before assignment to double). The code then attempts: static_cast<string>(42) to convert int to string, and static_cast<string>(3.14) to convert double to string. String to numeric conversions are also attempted: static_cast<int>("-3") and static_cast<double>("4.5"). These static_cast operations between numeric types and strings would produce errors. The correct approach for string conversions uses library functions: stoi() for string-to-int and stod() for string-to-double. The program demonstrates the results of each operation.

The key takeaway is that static_cast works between compatible numeric types (int to double, double to int) but does NOT work for converting between strings and numeric types. For those conversions, use to_string(), stoi(), stod() from the <string> library.

title: Casting Motivation
summary: Explains why casting is needed for correct division results, showing implicit casting with mixed types and explicit casting with static_cast and C-style casts.
main_text: Casting is defined as temporarily converting the type of a data value. What is the result of 5 + 3/2? The answer is 6 (because 3/2 = 1 in integer division), not 6.5. To achieve the correct answer for 5 + 3 / 2, you could use implicit casting (mixed expression) by writing 5 + 3.0 / 2. If an operator is applied to mixed type inputs, the less expressive type is automatically and implicitly cast (promoted) to the more expressive type (int is promoted to double). But what if instead of constants we have variables? int x=5, y=3, z=2; x + y/z; will not work (still integer division). We can perform an explicit cast using either C or C++ syntax: x + (double) y / z; (C style casting method) or x + static_cast<double>(y) / z; (C++ style casting method). BE CAREFUL: x + static_cast<double>(y/z); will NOT yield 6.5 because y/z is evaluated first as integer division (3/2 = 1), then 1 is cast to 1.0.
notes_text: The placement of the cast is critical. Casting must be applied BEFORE the division occurs - casting the numerator or denominator individually, not the result of the division. This is a very common mistake and exam question topic.

title: Common Casting Errors
summary: Warns that casting only changes type temporarily, only works on numeric types (not strings), and shows the correct string conversion functions.
main_text: Casting only changes the type temporarily for the sake of the expression (not a permanent type change). Casting only really works on numeric types and NOT strings. This is different from many other languages like Python. When converting to/from a string, do NOT use casting but functions from the string library: to_string(), stoi(), stod(), etc. The code example shows: double a = 3.6; int b = static_cast<int>(a) / 2; Works! b = 1 (casts 3.6 to 3, then 3/2 = 1), but a is still a double: 3.6. int c = 123; string d = static_cast<string>(c); Error! Does not compile. Instead use: string d = to_string(c); which Works! string e = "42"; int f = static_cast<int>(e); Error! Does not compile. Instead use: int f = stoi(e); (string-to-int). Use stod() for string-to-double. A visual diagram shows why static_cast<int>("42") fails: the string "42" is stored as bytes '4'(52), '2'(50), '\0'(00) - three bytes representing characters. The integer 42 is stored as bytes 00, 00, 00, 42 - a completely different binary representation. They are not interchangeable through casting.
notes_text: The memory layout diagram is key to understanding why casting between strings and numbers does not work. A string is an array of character bytes (ASCII codes), while an integer is a direct binary representation of the number. There is no simple bit reinterpretation that converts one to the other - you need a parsing function.

images.description: Memory layout comparison showing string '42' stored as character bytes (52, 50, 00) versus integer 42 stored as binary (00, 00, 00, 42), with a 'not equal' symbol between them

title: Understanding ASCII and chars
summary: Explains that char is an integer type using ASCII encoding, shows the full ASCII table, and demonstrates arithmetic and comparison operations on characters.
main_text: A char is just an integer type that is only 1 byte (limited range 0 to 255 or -128 to +127). cout uses the type, char or int, to infer if we want the ASCII character or integer value. We can perform arithmetic/comparison operations on ASCII chars since they are converted to integers. Code examples: char c = 'a'; is the same as char c = 97; cout << c << endl; prints 'a'. c = 97; cout << c << endl; still prints 'a' (because c is a char type). int x = c; cout << x << endl; prints 97 (because x is int type). char d = 'a' + 1; d now contains 98 (ASCII 'b'). cout << d << endl; prints 'b' on the screen. You can compare chars: if(c >= 'a' && c <= 'z') is equivalent to if(c >= 97 && c <= 122). x = '1'; cout << x << endl; prints 49 (ASCII value of '1'). The full ASCII printable characters table is shown with values 32-126 mapping to their characters.
notes_text: The ASCII table is a fundamental reference for C/C++ programming. Key ranges to remember: 48-57 are digits '0'-'9', 65-90 are uppercase 'A'-'Z', and 97-122 are lowercase 'a'-'z'. The difference between uppercase and lowercase is always 32 (e.g., 'A'=65, 'a'=97). Character arithmetic is used frequently for letter case conversion and digit extraction.

images.description: Complete ASCII printable characters table showing decimal values 32-126 mapped to their corresponding characters, organized in columns

title: Pre-/Post- Increment/Decrement
summary: Explains the ++ and -- operators, distinguishing between pre-increment/decrement (update before use) and post-increment/decrement (use then update).
main_text: Increment and decrement operators: ++ and -- (add and subtract 1). If ++ comes before a variable it is called pre-increment; if after, it is called post-increment. x++; if x was 2 it will be updated to 3 (x = x + 1). ++x; same as above (no difference when not in a larger expression). x--; if x was 2 it will be updated to 1 (x = x - 1). --x; same as above (no difference when not in a larger expression). The difference between pre- and post- is only evident when used in a larger expression. Pre: Update (inc./dec.) the variable before using it in the expression. Post: Use the old value of the variable in the expression then update (inc./dec.) it. Examples (starting with int y; int x = 3; for each): y = x++ + 5; Post-inc: Use x=3 in expr then inc. Result: y=8, x=4. y = ++x + 5; Pre-inc: Inc x=4 first, then use in expr. Result: y=9, x=4. y = x-- + 5; Post-dec: Use x=3 in expr then dec. Result: y=8, x=2. y = --x + 5; Pre-dec: Dec x=2 first, then use in expr. Result: y=7, x=2.
notes_text: While understanding pre/post increment is important, many style guides discourage using them in complex expressions because they make code harder to read. In standalone statements (x++; or ++x;), there is no difference. The distinction only matters when the expression's value is used, such as in assignment or function arguments.

title: Library Functions
summary: Code example demonstrating common C++ library functions including cos, pow, sqrt, abs, min, atoi, and atof with their required headers.
main_text: This slide shows a complete program using various library functions. Required headers: #include <iostream>, #include <cmath>, #include <algorithm>, #include <cstdlib>, #include <string>. The program demonstrates: cos(M_PI) returns the cosine of pi (M_PI is a predefined constant). pow(2,3) returns 2 to the 3rd power = 8. sqrt(100) returns the square root of 100 = 10. abs(-3) returns the absolute value of -3 = 3. min(-5, -2) returns the smaller of -5 and -2 = -5. atoi("103")+1 converts the C-string "103" to integer and adds 1 = 104. atof("1.25")+2.5 converts the C-string "1.25" to double and adds 2.5 = 3.75. Each result is printed using cout.
notes_text: Students should be aware of which header file provides each function. atoi and atof are C-style functions from <cstdlib> that work on C-strings. For C++ std::string objects, use stoi() and stod() from <string> instead. M_PI may not be available on all compilers without special flags.

images.description: C++ program calling various library functions (cos, pow, sqrt, abs, min, atoi, atof) with their results printed to cout

title: Math and Other Library Functions
summary: Reference for common C++ library functions (sqrt, pow, sin/cos/tan, abs, max/min) with their headers and usage examples.
main_text: C++ predefines a variety of functions. Common functions include: sqrt(x) returns the square root of x (in <cmath>). pow(x, y) returns x^y, or x to the power y (in <cmath>). sin(x)/cos(x)/tan(s) returns the sine/cosine/tangent of x if x is in radians (in <cmath>). abs(x) returns the absolute value of x (in <cstdlib>). max(x, y) and min(x, y) returns the maximum/minimum of x and y (in <algorithm>). You call these by writing them similarly to how you would use a function in mathematics, using parentheses for the inputs (aka arguments). The result is replaced into the bigger expression. You must #include the correct library - #includes tell the compiler about the various pre-defined functions that your program may choose to call. Code example: double res = cos(0); gives res = 1.0. res = sqrt(2) / 2; gives res = 1.414/2 = 0.707. cout << max(34, 56) << endl; outputs 56.
notes_text: Knowing which header provides each function is important for compilation. cmath provides mathematical functions, algorithm provides general-purpose algorithms like min/max/sort, cstdlib provides utility functions like abs/atoi/rand. The reference at cplusplus.com/reference/cmath/ has comprehensive documentation.

images.description: Code example showing library function calls in assignments and expressions, demonstrating how function return values are used inline

title: #include Directive
summary: Explains how #include works for C and C++ header files, with a reference table mapping C headers to their C++ equivalents.
main_text: Common usage: To include 'header files' that allow us to access functions defined in a separate file or library. For pure C compilers, we include a C header file with its filename: #include <stdlib.h>. For C++ compilers, we include a C header file without the .h extension and prepend a 'c': #include <cstdlib>. The reference table maps C to C++ headers: stdio.h/cstdio provides C Input/Output/File access (printf, fopen, snprintf, etc.), while iostream provides C++ I/O and File streams (cin, cout, cerr). stdlib.h/cstdlib provides rand(), Memory allocation, etc., while algorithm provides common data processing tasks/algorithms (find, sort, min/max). string.h/cstring provides C-string library functions that operate on character arrays, while string provides the C++ string class that defines the 'string' object. math.h/cmath provides Math functions like sin(), pow(), etc., while vector provides the C++ array-like container class.
notes_text: Understanding the relationship between C and C++ headers helps when reading older code or working with C libraries in C++ programs. The C++ versions (prefixed with 'c') place their contents in the std namespace, while the C versions (.h suffix) place them in the global namespace.
