title: Random Number Generator
summary: Code example demonstrating the rand() function from cstdlib with optional srand() seeding, generating pseudo-random integers.
main_text: This slide shows a C++ program that generates random numbers using the rand() function. The program includes <iostream>, <cstdlib>, and <ctime>. Inside main(): Two commented-out lines show seeding options: srand(42) for a fixed seed, and srand(time(0)) for a time-based seed. The program prints RAND_MAX (the maximum value rand() can return) and then calls rand() four times, printing each result. Without calling srand(), the program will produce the same sequence of numbers every time it runs. The rand() function is declared/prototyped in <cstdlib>.
notes_text: The rand() function is a legacy C function. Modern C++ provides better random number generation through the <random> header with std::mt19937 and distribution classes. However, rand() is simpler to learn and sufficient for introductory courses.

images.description: C++ program showing four calls to rand() with commented-out srand() seeding options, printing the RAND_MAX value and four random numbers

title: rand() and RAND_MAX
summary: Explains how rand() works, its range (0 to RAND_MAX), and how to use it for coin flips and generating uniform random fractions.
main_text: (Pseudo)random number generation [(P)RNG] in C is accomplished with the rand() function declared/prototyped in cstdlib. rand() returns an integer between 0 and RAND_MAX. RAND_MAX is an integer constant defined in <cstdlib>. How could you generate a value that simulates the flip of a coin (i.e. 2 outcomes: 0 or 1 with equal probability)? Use: int r; r = rand(); if(r < RAND_MAX/2){ cout << "Heads"; } This checks if the random value falls in the lower half of the range. How could you generate a fraction (decimal) with uniform probability of being between [0,1]? Use: double r; r = static_cast<double>(rand()) / RAND_MAX; This casts rand()'s integer result to double before dividing by RAND_MAX, producing a value between 0.0 and 1.0. The number line diagram shows 0 on the left and RAND_MAX on the right, illustrating the full range of rand() output.
notes_text: The static_cast is essential in the fraction generation formula. Without it, rand()/RAND_MAX would perform integer division and always return 0 (since rand() is always less than or equal to RAND_MAX). Casting to double first ensures floating-point division.

images.description: Number line showing the range of rand() from 0 to RAND_MAX, illustrating the full output range of the random number generator

title: Seeding Random Number Generator
summary: Explains why srand() is needed to get different random sequences, recommending srand(time(0)) called once at program start.
main_text: Re-running a program that calls rand() will generate the same sequence of random numbers (i.e. each run will be exactly the same). If we want each execution of the program to be different then we need to seed the RNG with a different value. srand(int seed) is a function in <cstdlib> to seed the RNG with the value of seed. Unless seed changes from execution to execution, we will still have the same problem. Solution: Seed it with the day and time (returned by the time() function defined in ctime). srand(time(0)); - only do this once at the start of the program. Then: int r = rand(); (now call rand() as many times as you want), int r2 = rand(); (another random number). The sequence of random numbers will be different for each execution of the program. Important: Only call srand() ONCE at the start of the program, not each time you want to call rand()! The approximate rand() function is shown: val = ((val * 1103515245) + 12345) % RAND_MAX; This reveals that rand() is deterministic - given the same seed, it produces the same sequence.
notes_text: The internal formula for rand() shows why it is called 'pseudo-random' - it is actually a deterministic mathematical sequence. The seed determines the starting point of this sequence. Calling srand() before every rand() call would reset the sequence, potentially giving the same values if called in quick succession (since time(0) has only 1-second resolution).

title: You're Just My Type - Solutions

The table shows each constant, the type it was paired with, and the correct answer: 4.0 paired with int is WRONG - it is actually a double (the .0 makes it a double). 5 paired with int is RIGHT - it is an int. 'a' paired with string is WRONG - it is a char (single quotes denote char). "abc" paired with string is WRONG in a sense - it is technically a C-string (double quotes create a C-string literal, not a C++ string object, though conversion is automatic). 5. paired with double is RIGHT - the decimal point makes it a float/double (. = non-integer). 5 paired with char is WRONG - it is an int, but if you store 5 in a char variable it would be okay since char is just a small number that fits in 8-bits/1-byte. "5.0" paired with double is WRONG - it is a C-string (double quotes mean string, regardless of content). '5' paired with int is WRONG - it is a char (single quotes always denote char).

title: cin Question - Detailed Solution
summary: Shows the detailed solution to the cin type mismatch question with step-by-step stream state diagrams showing how cin parses mismatched input types.
main_text:
This slide provides the detailed solution to the cin question about type mismatches. The program reads: int x; cin >> x; with user typing '1.5 42'. cin reads 1 into x (stops at '.'), leaving '.5 42
' in the stream. Then double y, z; cin >> y >> z; reads .5 into y and 42 into z from the remaining stream. Then string s; cin >> s; with user typing '103.25'. cin reads '103.25' as a string (stops at whitespace). The step-by-step stream state is shown: After first cin >> x: x = 1, stream has '.5 42
'. After cin >> y >> z: y = 0.5, z = 42, stream has '
'. The user then types '103.25
'. After cin >> s: s = "103.25". Final output: x = (not shown), y,z = 0.5 42 (implied), s = 103.25. Key insight: when cin reads for string, numeric digits are just regular characters - it reads all characters until whitespace.
notes_text: This detailed walkthrough of stream state is essential for understanding cin behavior. The fact that cin >> int stops at a decimal point and leaves it in the stream creates a cascading effect where subsequent reads consume the fractional part. This behavior is deterministic and predictable once understood.

title: Parts of C/C++ Variables
summary: Describes the four parts of a variable: type, name/identifier, location (address), and value, with naming conventions (camelCase and snake_case).
main_text: Variables have a: type [int, char, unsigned int, float, double, etc.], name/identifier that the programmer will use to reference the value in that memory location [e.g. x, numStudents, is_high_enough, etc.]. Identifiers must start with [A-Z, a-z, or an underscore '_'] and can then contain any alphanumeric character [0-9, A-Z, a-z, _] (but no punctuation other than underscores). Use descriptive names (e.g. numStudents, doneFlag). Avoid cryptic names (myvar1, a_thing). Variables also have a location [the address in memory where it is allocated] and a value. Naming conventions: Camel case capitalizes the first letter of each word (with the possible exception of the first word): numStudents, isHighEnough. Snake case separates each word with an underscore '_': num_students, is_high_enough. Reminder: You must declare a variable before using it. Code example: int quantity = 4; double cost = 5.75; cout << quantity*cost << endl; Here 'quantity' has name 'quantity', address 1008412, and value 4; 'cost' has address 287144 and value 5.75.
notes_text: Good naming conventions make code self-documenting. Both camelCase and snake_case are widely used in C++. The C++ standard library uses snake_case, while many game engines and frameworks use camelCase. What matters most is consistency within a project.

images.description: Diagram showing two variables (quantity and cost) with their names, addresses (1008412 and 287144), and values (4 and 5.75) illustrated as labeled memory boxes

title: Choosing Your Type
summary: Flowchart decision tree for selecting the appropriate C++ data type based on what kind of data needs to be stored.
main_text: The flowchart starts with the question 'What am I storing?' and branches into three categories: Number, Text/Character(s) for display, and Logical (true/false) value. For Numbers: 'What kind of number is it?' branches to 'Contains a decimal/fractional value' (use a double, examples: 3.0, -3.14159, 7.5) or 'Integer' which further asks 'What range of values might it use?' - 'Positive only' leads to unsigned int/size_t (examples: 0, 2147682), 'Possibly negative' leads to int (examples: 0, -2147682, 2147682). For Text/Character(s): 'Is it a single char or many (i.e. a string of chars)?' - 'Single' leads to char (examples: 'a', '1', '.'), 'Many' leads to string (examples: "Hi", "2022"). For Logical value: use bool (examples: true, false).
notes_text: This decision tree is a practical tool for beginners. When unsure which type to use, follow the branches: numbers with decimals get double, whole positive numbers get unsigned int, whole numbers that might be negative get int, single characters get char, text gets string, and yes/no values get bool.

images.description: Decision tree flowchart showing how to select the appropriate C++ data type based on the nature of the data being stored, with branches for numbers, text, and logical values

title: Preprocessor and Directives
summary: Explains the C/C++ preprocessor, #include for inserting file contents, and #define for text substitution macros.
main_text: Preprocessor directives are somewhat unique to C/C++. The compiler will scan through C code looking for directives (e.g. #include, #define, anything else that starts with '#'). The preprocessor performs textual changes, substitutions, insertions, etc. before actual compilation. #include <filename> or #include "filename" inserts the entire contents of 'filename' into the given C text file. The angle brackets search system include directories, while double quotes search the local directory first. #define find_pattern replace_pattern replaces any occurrence of find_pattern with replace_pattern throughout the code. Example: #define PI 3.14159 means that wherever PI appears in the code (x = PI;), the preprocessor replaces it with the literal value (x = 3.14159;) before compilation.
notes_text: #define macros are a legacy C feature. In modern C++, prefer 'const double PI = 3.14159;' or 'constexpr double PI = 3.14159;' over #define because const variables are type-safe and respect scope rules, while #define is a simple text substitution that can cause subtle bugs.

title: I Do Declare - C++ vs Python Variable Declaration
summary: Compares C++ and Python variable handling: C++ requires declaration before use, variables hold garbage if uninitialized, and types cannot change.
main_text: Unlike Python, you must do a one-time declaration of a variable before using it in C++. If not initialized via assignment ('='), variables will NOT default to a value like 0, but will contain random data/garbage. Good practice: always initialize your variables. C++ is a strongly-typed language; Python is too, but C++ has more restrictions. You cannot change what type of value the variable stores - in C++ a variable name corresponds to a reserved, fixed-size memory location. The C++ code example shows: x = 5; is an error (x assigned before declaration). int x; declares x but it is uninitialized (garbage). x = x+1; is BAD because x is still uninitialized garbage. x = 1; initializes x's value to 1. double y = 3.14; x = "pi is"; is an error because x was declared as int and cannot be assigned a string. Comparison with Python: def main(): x = 5 (stores integer), y = 3.14, x = "pi is" (x changes to store a string) - all valid in Python. C++ is 'strongly-typed' and requires variables to be declared before being used. Python does not require explicitly declaring and typing a variable.
notes_text: The comparison with Python highlights fundamental differences in language design philosophy. Python's dynamic typing is convenient but can hide type-related bugs until runtime. C++'s static typing catches these errors at compile time, which is safer but requires more explicit code. The memory diagram shows why types are fixed: int x reserves exactly 4 bytes at a specific address.

These are the three integer types we will use 99% of the time (char, int, unsigned int highlighted).
